correctness.rationale: The generalized coefficient valuation is a difference of cyclic interval sums. When an exponent word has period T, exact cancellation of complete T-blocks reduces every possible length to remainders 1 through T-1. The four induced column exponent words and their 16 minimum-prefix claims are directly reconstructed from (0,1,1,0,2); multiples of five yield an all-zero column. For any positive-integer periodic sequence with period <=4, primewise integrality of the first, second or third columns gives A=B at period three, and A=C together with B<=D at period four; these imply the divisibility chain in every residue class. Independent direct recomputation from the packaged code checks these finite premises; finite tests are not used as an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The motivating paper asks about higher-order recurrence divisibility, but its known nondivisible counterexample fails the second column. The later binomid-index extension literature addresses first-level integrality and periodic first-level exponent words, without proving that all columns are binomid or that five is a sharp period boundary. Thus the mathematical implication comparison against full relevant sources supports a distinct all-level theorem, subject to the stated residual risk.
residual_risks: A differently phrased or unindexed classification of all-level periodic binomid sequences may exist; bibliographic search cannot prove absolute uniqueness.
The theorem is for pure periods and makes no assertion about eventual-periodicity or the separate order-two recurrence question.

value.rationale: The all-column property is appreciably stronger than binomid integrality for one column. An explicit nondivisible but all-level sequence directly treats the higher-order branch of Shapiro’s published question. The proof additionally classifies the short-period boundary for all positive integer sequences, not just prime-power special examples: periods 1–4 necessarily force index divisibility, while period five admits failure. The threshold therefore has an intrinsic minimality motivation.
